answerChoices.label: Plan posterior inguinal-wall reinforcement
answerChoices.rationale: The dynamic medial bulge and activity limitation support elective repair of the posterior-wall defect, rather than treating static cord fat as the symptomatic lesion.

answerChoices.label: Plan deep-ring exploration and sac repair
answerChoices.rationale: The earlier cord-fat report invites anchoring on an indirect sac, but that is not the structure changing during strain.

answerChoices.label: Plan observation with scheduled groin review
answerChoices.rationale: Observation is credible for a reducible inguinal hernia with little functional burden; recurrent interruption of work changes that balance.

decisionNodes.explanation: The changing medial posterior-wall bulge, rather than the static fat finding, identifies the symptomatic direct defect. Reducibility establishes a nonemergency setting; it does not make observation preferable when symptoms repeatedly limit work. Plan elective posterior-wall repair after normal surgical assessment. The item does not prescribe a particular mesh, approach or fixation technique.

decisionNodes.explanation: Separate route from composition. Retain adequate oral energy/protein while restricting long-chain triglycerides and enriching medium-chain triglycerides, with output, fluid, electrolyte and nutritional monitoring. The diet chronology is a reason to reassess, not proof that one ingredient caused the entire output change.

cues.phrase: Recurrent distension and vomiting; feeds returned to the previous rate
cues.why: Directly supplies why the increase-feeds option has already failed.

cues.phrase: anticipated several more days of restricted delivery
cues.why: Preinterprets persistence and rehearses why waiting at the current rate is inadequate.

cues.phrase: Add parenteral nutrition to the prescribed tube regimen
cues.why: Only the key remedies the conspicuous large deficit while preserving the only tolerated route; alternatives repeat the failed escalation or leave the deficit unchanged.

fairness: Supplemental PN is defensible in this malnourished patient with persistent inadequate delivery. The current rate, target and trajectory are useful clinical facts, but they eliminate both distractors almost verbatim; there is little remaining judgment.

Importance: very high-yield perioperative nutrition. Realism: inpatient decision reviewed later in clinic is coherent. The task should distinguish historical care from a present clinic order. Too easy for PGY-2/3 residents; no definite key error identified.
suggestions: Retain actual intake and intolerance, but compare credible supplemental-PN/enteral strategies rather than a known failed rate increase and prolonged severe underfeeding.
If timing is the objective, supply the verified time-course and nutritional-risk criteria and test a genuine near-boundary decision without inventing thresholds.

qualityReview.counterfactual: No tolerated gastrointestinal delivery would favor exclusive PN; an adequately nourished patient would not have this same refeeding-risk inference.

clinicalCase.presentation: Evan Ross, a 67-year-old man, reviews his hospital feeding record in postoperative clinic. Before colectomy he had weeks of very little intake, progressive weight loss and muscle wasting. On postoperative day ten he remained dependent on nasogastric decompression. A small postpyloric feed had just been started; the nutrition team was planning additional delivery.

decisionNodes.stem: Which nutrition-start plan best fits Evan Ross's recorded stage of care?

answerChoices.label: Supplemental PN and thiamine before escalation
answerChoices.rationale: Limited tolerated enteral delivery can be retained while PN fills the deficit. Severe preceding undernutrition warrants thiamine before restarting substantial nutrition and close electrolyte monitoring.

answerChoices.label: Exclusive PN and thiamine before escalation
answerChoices.rationale: This recognizes refeeding risk but unnecessarily discards a tolerated gastrointestinal contribution.

answerChoices.label: Supplemental PN and thiamine after hypophosphatemia
answerChoices.rationale: This recognizes the delivery gap but incorrectly waits for a biochemical complication before planned thiamine supplementation.

answerChoices.label: Exclusive PN and thiamine after hypophosphatemia
answerChoices.rationale: This both abandons the tolerated route and delays the preventive vitamin step.

decisionNodes.explanation: Persistent restricted delivery in a malnourished patient supports supplemental PN while retaining tolerated enteral nutrition. A normal starting phosphate does not erase the preceding undernutrition or justify waiting for hypophosphatemia before preventive thiamine. Plan thiamine before substantial additional delivery and monitor clinical status and electrolytes. No fixed PN dose, advancement rate or stopping threshold is taught.

priorIndependentReview.title: Mesh after a controlled enterotomy
fairness: One defensible best implant among these options: the learner must interpret the controlled contamination, viable repair and separable retromuscular plane, then apply material selection rather than reflexively choose biologic mesh. The observations are necessary eligibility information, not an answer-label match.

Importance: high-yield abdominal-wall practice and examination content. Realism: a single-stage intraoperative implant decision reviewed in clinic is credible; options name parallel, specific implants. The record does not imply that every enterotomy mandates immediate synthetic mesh.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. This is an offline editorial judgment, not verification of current comparative evidence or clinical approval.
suggestions: Retain the controlled contamination and tissue-plane details and have Melissa confirm the exact mesh-material ranking for the stated operative circumstances. No wording repair is required for editorial acceptance.

concept.learningObjective: Choose the supported mesh material when a selected single-stage ventral repair proceeds after securely repaired enterotomy with adequate source control and minimal contamination.
concept.novelty: Adds an unadmitted material-selection objective; the active construct decides fascial closure rather than implant material in controlled contamination.
concept.conceptVersionReason: Same scored clinical decision and stable FSRS identity; new observations/options require application rather than the earlier recall or cue shortcut.
concept.historyMigration: None. Preserved meanings retain IDs; materially changed constructs use new IDs and leave old histories intact.

clinicalCase.presentation: Martin Hayes, a 59-year-old man, reviews the hospital plan for his incisional-hernia repair. During adhesiolysis a small-bowel opening was recognized and closed. The record describes pink perfused bowel, a dry closure on repeated inspection and a small amount of immediately suctioned enteric fluid. The posterior layer could be closed between bowel and the retromuscular implant, and the anterior fascia could be approximated.

decisionNodes.stem: Which implant plan best fits Martin Hayes's documented single-stage reconstruction?

answerChoices.label: Retromuscular macroporous monofilament synthetic mesh
answerChoices.rationale: The observations describe the controlled-enterotomy scope in which permanent macroporous monofilament synthetic mesh remains a supported selection.

answerChoices.label: Retromuscular non-cross-linked biologic tissue mesh
answerChoices.rationale: A repaired enterotomy is not by itself a reason to substitute biologic material for the supported synthetic selection in this reconstruction.

answerChoices.label: Retromuscular microporous multifilament synthetic mesh
answerChoices.rationale: The recorded material recommendation distinguishes pore/filament structure; a permanent synthetic label does not make these materials equivalent.

decisionNodes.explanation: Infer the contamination and repair context from observations rather than the phrase source control complete. cues.phrase: The pale disrupted areas extended around the base onto both sides of the ileal tube.
cues.why: The presentation supplies the full extent before the schematic is interpreted. With both opposing walls involved, the only whole-segment resection is the obvious coverage answer.

cues.phrase: Disrupted wall is marked around the diverticular base and on both the antimesenteric and opposite mesenteric sides of an adjacent ileal segment.
cues.why: The necessary accessible description reinforces the same coverage puzzle; wedge and base-only excision cannot encompass the explicitly bilateral extent. This is not a reason to remove accessible findings.

fairness: Segmental resection is defensible for this distribution, but the key also commits to primary anastomosis without circulation, contamination or remaining bowel-perfusion context. 'Healthy' ends in the drawing do not establish all reconstruction conditions.

Importance: useful general-surgery resection judgment. Realism: the image exists and is readable, but 'pale/disrupted' conflates observations with different implications; specify the actual operative wall injury or viability finding. Too easy as a lesion-coverage exercise.
suggestions: Ask resection extent without adding an unsupported reconstruction commitment, or supply the observations required to choose anastomosis.

decisionNodes.stem: Which resection extent best fits Adam Stone's recorded operative findings?

answerChoices.label: Segmental small-bowel resection
answerChoices.rationale: The disease crosses into the ileum, and a local base closure would distort the lumen. Bowel-inclusive segmental resection addresses both findings.

answerChoices.label: Wedge resection with transverse closure
answerChoices.rationale: A bowel-inclusive wedge can be reasonable for localized base disease when the remaining lumen and tissue permit it; the closure observation changes that ranking here.

answerChoices.label: Diverticulectomy across the base
answerChoices.rationale: A tip-limited lesion in a long narrow diverticulum can be treated more locally; that would not address the represented base/ileal disease.

decisionNodes.explanation: Choose extent from both disease distribution and the effect of closure. Base/adjacent-ileal disease defeats simple diverticulectomy, while the observed lumen distortion makes a local wedge unattractive. Segmental ileal resection is the best extent among these choices. Reconstruction is deliberately a separate decision; no primary-anastomosis commitment is implied by the color observations.

priorIndependentReview.title: Celiac serology when IgA is deficient
fairness: The balanced two-by-two choices avoid convergence. IgA deficiency invalidates the reassuring IgA result, while gluten withdrawal separately limits a repeat antibody evaluation. The learner must address both assay selection and testing conditions; neither answer component is uniquely repeated or explained in the stem.
Importance: useful diagnostic-validity and nutrition content, though less central to operative general surgery than the perioperative items. Realism: plausible in a surgical nutrition clinic.

The key is defensible among the offered blood-testing plans. It does not establish a complete celiac diagnostic pathway or a universal gluten-challenge regimen; suitability and supervision require clinical review. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline.
suggestions: Keep both competing validity problems and the balanced options. At clinical sign-off, confirm how supervised gluten reintroduction is represented; do not add an unsupported dose or duration.

decisionNodes.stem: Which diagnostic blood-testing plan should Priya Shah's team arrange?

answerChoices.label: tTG-IgG/deamidated gliadin peptide IgG assay panel with gluten reintroduction
answerChoices.rationale: This corrects both the antibody-class limitation and the changed exposure that can suppress disease-test findings. A specialist directs the exposure plan; no challenge dose or interval is specified.

answerChoices.label: tTG-IgG/deamidated gliadin peptide IgG assay panel with continued gluten avoidance
answerChoices.rationale: The antibody class is changed appropriately, but the shared dietary limitation in disease testing remains.

answerChoices.label: tTG-IgA/endomysial IgA assay panel with gluten reintroduction
answerChoices.rationale: The exposure is addressed, but both assays still depend on an immunoglobulin class below detection.

answerChoices.label: tTG-IgA/endomysial IgA assay panel with continued gluten avoidance
answerChoices.rationale: This preserves both limitations in the negative result: deficient IgA and restricted testing exposure.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret two independent preanalytic conditions before replacing the test. Switching to IgG does not repair gluten withdrawal, and restoring exposure does not repair absent IgA. The named IgG panel with specialist-directed reintroduction addresses both. Further adult confirmation follows the results; no universal challenge dose or duration is invented.

answerChoices.label: Human leukocyte antigen testing before gluten challenge
answerChoices.rationale: Typing can first identify a result that makes celiac disease very unlikely without requiring gluten exposure. A compatible result does not diagnose disease and leaves supervised challenge/testing to discuss.

answerChoices.label: Supervised gluten challenge before serology and biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: This can establish disease when appropriate, but bypasses a useful exposure-independent preliminary test in this patient's circumstances.

answerChoices.rationale: Biopsy while restriction continues can remain nondiagnostic and does not answer the susceptibility question before a potentially burdensome challenge.

decisionNodes.explanation: The negative restricted-diet studies do not establish that disease is absent. Susceptibility typing is unaffected by dietary withdrawal and can identify a DQ2/DQ8-negative result that makes celiac disease very unlikely. A compatible result establishes susceptibility, not active disease; further confirmation may still require a supervised gluten challenge followed by appropriate testing. No universal challenge dose or duration is supplied.

cues.phrase: The complete specimen list from an outside mucosal-biopsy procedure identifies antral mucosa and esophageal squamous tissue.
cues.why: The conspicuous wrong-site specimen list points to the only option that obtains tissue at a new intestinal site.

cues.phrase: Assay panel for repeat tTG-IgA and endomysial IgA
cues.why: The word 'repeat' and already-positive tTG make this look like redundant work, while the key is the only tissue acquisition.

fairness: Duodenal biopsy is a defensible next step, but the HLA result is largely decorative: the same answer follows from symptoms, positive tTG with normal IgA, and lack of duodenal sampling. The title's susceptibility-typing construct is not meaningfully assessed.

Importance: moderately useful diagnostic-workup content; weaker general-surgery yield than the other nutrition questions. Realism: an outside endoscopy can miss the relevant target, but the record should make clear why that endoscopy was performed. Too easy; the tissue versus assay category split assists selection.
suggestions: Choose whether the objective is interpreting HLA or obtaining adequate duodenal tissue. For the latter, compare credible specimen/acquisition strategies with an actual adequacy discrepancy; for the former, make HLA change the next decision.
Avoid using two blood panels as disposable foils for the sole biopsy choice. Consider merging with the other celiac diagnostic-validity items.

decisionNodes.stem: Which diagnostic plan should precede Olivia Park's dietary prescription?

answerChoices.label: Obtain tTG-IgA during gluten exposure
answerChoices.rationale: Normal total IgA supports the usual IgA-based initial pathway. Genetic susceptibility and an isolated IgG result do not replace that evaluation.

answerChoices.label: Obtain deamidated gliadin peptide IgG
answerChoices.rationale: This is a credible alternative assay when IgA deficiency limits the usual pathway, but normal total IgA does not establish that indication.

answerChoices.label: Obtain tTG-IgA after gluten withdrawal
answerChoices.rationale: This uses the relevant assay but changes the testing conditions before diagnostic confirmation.

decisionNodes.explanation: HLA-DQ2 identifies susceptibility rather than active disease. With normal total IgA and ongoing gluten exposure, obtain the usual tTG-IgA assessment before prescribing withdrawal; subsequent adult confirmation follows the findings. IgG assays have a selected role when IgA deficiency makes the usual tests unreliable. This does not dismiss the symptoms or establish that a positive IgG can never be informative.

priorIndependentReview.title: HCC tumor burden versus liver resection suitability
fairness: The learner must distinguish limited tumor burden from liver functional reserve and clinically important portal hypertension, then prioritize a pathway addressing both. A small solitary tumor makes resection or ablation initially credible; repeated ascites drainage and varices change the ranking.

Importance: high-yield HPB decision-making. Realism: an outpatient transplant referral discussion is appropriate. 'Assessment' rather than guaranteed transplantation properly leaves candidacy evaluation open.

Transplant-center assessment is the best priority among the options. Ablation could still have a bridging or alternative role; the question should not imply that choosing assessment prohibits it. No definite key error identified offline.
suggestions: Preserve the tumor-versus-liver-function tension and the word 'prioritized'. Have clinical sign-off retain the distinction between referral priority, final candidacy and possible bridging treatment.

concept.displayName: HCC tumor burden versus liver resection suitability

concept.novelty: The existing combined favorable-profile case selects resection; this construct resolves a clinically different discordance between small tumor burden and poor liver reserve.

clinicalCase.displayName: HCC tumor burden versus liver resection suitability
clinicalCase.presentation: Samuel Green, a 58-year-old man, comes to clinic after liver-tumor staging. He has required repeated ascites drainage, has esophageal varices on endoscopy and a platelet count below the laboratory interval. He remains independent in daily activities.

priorIndependentReview.title: Structural assessment before gastric emptying

cues.phrase: The scope stopped proximal to the narrowing.
cues.why: Names the incomplete inspection that the key proposes to finish.

cues.phrase: The specimen log identifies tissue from a prepyloric erosion, while CT describes focal thickening at the narrowing.
cues.why: The overt sample/lesion mismatch steers to the only option that includes lesion biopsy. It is clinically relevant, but combined with nonbiopsy competitors largely announces the missing action.

fairness: Importance: high-yield distinction between mechanical outlet obstruction and a motility diagnosis. The intended two steps are recognizing that diabetes does not establish gastroparesis and resolving an inadequately sampled structural lesion.

Fairness concern: the record does not explain why the first scope stopped or what makes a second endoscopy feasible and diagnostically superior now. Contrast fluoroscopy can be a defensible next anatomical study after an incompletely traversed outlet. I cannot confidently rank that sequence without more acquisition/obstruction context.

Realism: retained food, narrowing and focal thickening are credible. Repeat inspection and tissue sampling may be appropriate, but the needed preparation or altered technique is not specified; do not infer it from the key.
suggestions: Give the actual reason the first examination was limited and the observations establishing safe, useful repeat access. Specify the repeat diagnostic protocol if it differs materially.
Compare credible approaches to the unresolved lesion at the same stage, and retain the distinction between prepyloric tissue and the actual target without turning it into a missing-biopsy slogan.

qualityReview.counterfactual: A completed normal outlet examination would favor gastric-emptying testing; complete obstruction or unsafe endoscopic access would alter the sequence.

decisionNodes.stem: Which diagnostic plan should the hospital use next for Peter Bell's vomiting?

answerChoices.label: Repeat endoscopy with pyloric biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: The first procedure ended because of retained contents, not an impassable proven stricture. Decompression changes the acquisition conditions, and the irregular structural lesion warrants direct assessment and tissue.

answerChoices.label: Contrast fluoroscopy with pyloric transit mapping
answerChoices.rationale: Fluoroscopy can characterize transit, but contrast already passes and it would not characterize the irregular mural lesion histologically.

answerChoices.label: Prepared four-hour gastric-emptying scintigraphy
answerChoices.rationale: This is the appropriate physiology protocol after structural exclusion; diabetes and retained food do not supply that prerequisite.

decisionNodes.explanation: Retained food in diabetes does not establish gastroparesis. The first examination was preparation-limited; decompression and persistent contrast passage support a prepared repeat examination rather than treating prior termination as proof that endoscopic access is impossible. Assess and sample the irregular pyloric lesion before moving to emptying physiology. This is a diagnostic plan, not an instruction to force a scope through a tight obstruction.

cues.phrase: the supplements she actually consumed
cues.why: Emphasizes exactly which numbers the reader should add, preempting the proposed counting error.

cues.phrase: Retain PN as the primary route; reduce meals and supplements
cues.why: Makes the competing plan reduce a tolerated route that already supplies the target, so it is weak even without detailed nutrition knowledge.

cues.phrase: Replace the drinks with postpyloric tube feeding
cues.why: Adds an invasive route despite explicitly tolerated meals and consumed drinks. This is a category/invasiveness cue rather than a close clinical alternative.

fairness: The oral totals exceed the stated energy and protein targets, and PN withdrawal is defensible. The table is basic addition, followed by an obvious route choice; it does not meet the intended resident difficulty.

Importance: high-yield transition off PN. Realism: a dietitian intake audit is appropriate in recovery clinic. No definite clinical error identified, but the task should distinguish withdrawing the prescription from any particular tapering or glucose-monitoring protocol. Too easy.
suggestions: Compare plausible PN reduction or withdrawal plans with the same oral regimen, using an intake trajectory or clinically relevant limitation that changes the decision.
Remove the didactic emphasis on 'actually consumed'; keep recorded delivered intake as neutral data. Avoid making tube feeding a foil when oral tolerance is unambiguously established.

priorIndependentReview.title: Incidental gallbladder muscle invasion

cues.phrase: the cystic-duct margin is free of tumor
cues.why: This directly weakens the duct-stump re-excision distractor. It is necessary operative-planning information, however, and does not select completion resection over surveillance without interpreting invasion depth.

fairness: The learner must reinterpret the histological layer despite the original 'superficial' label, then distinguish completion oncologic assessment from surveillance. The key requests specialist assessment rather than declaring an operation inevitable.
Importance: high-yield incidental gallbladder-cancer management. Realism: specialist slide review, staging and functional assessment fit a postoperative clinic visit.

The key is defensible among these choices. T1b completion-resection recommendations and patient-specific tradeoffs require clinician confirmation; offline editorial PASS is not a claim that all evidence is uniform. The negative duct margin is a justified cue, not a reason to omit a necessary finding.
suggestions: Retain the raw muscle-invasion finding and specialist-assessment framing. Preserve margin and staging information. Confirm the exact completion-resection recommendation at clinical sign-off.

concept.learningObjective: Recognize muscular invasion as outside the completely resected T1a observation pathway and obtain hepatobiliary surgical review.
concept.novelty: The active objective permits completed T1a excision; this new referral construct concerns documented muscular invasion and does not prescribe an unverified extended operation.
concept.conceptVersionReason: Same scored clinical decision and stable FSRS identity; new observations/options require application rather than the earlier recall or cue shortcut.
concept.historyMigration: None. Preserved meanings retain IDs; materially changed constructs use new IDs and leave old histories intact.

clinicalCase.presentation: Teresa Wood, a 69-year-old woman, returns after cholecystectomy. The original summary called the incidental carcinoma superficial. On specialist slide review, tumor nests are present within smooth-muscle bundles beneath the lamina propria; the cystic-duct margin is free of tumor. Staging CT shows no distant disease. She walks to the shops and climbs the stairs at home without cardiopulmonary symptoms.

decisionNodes.stem: Which postoperative cancer-planning sequence best fits Teresa Wood's revised pathology?

answerChoices.label: HPB assessment of completion oncologic resection
answerChoices.rationale: Muscular invasion is outside the completely removed T1a observation pathway. The staging/fitness information makes assessment of completion oncologic surgery the remaining planning question; this is not an automatic operation.

answerChoices.label: HPB assessment of post-cholecystectomy surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: A clear cystic-duct margin does not make smooth-muscle invasion equivalent to a completely resected lamina-propria-limited tumor.

answerChoices.label: HPB assessment of duct-stump re-excision
answerChoices.rationale: This directs the next workup to an involved duct margin, whereas the actual changed finding is depth in the gallbladder wall, with a clear duct margin.

decisionNodes.explanation: First interpret the wall layer rather than the word superficial, then distinguish depth-driven reassessment from a duct-margin problem. This is T1b muscular invasion, so the completely resected T1a pathway cannot be applied. HPB assessment of completion surgery is the specific next planning issue; this draft does not prescribe an unverified hepatic or nodal extent.

priorIndependentReview.title: Gastric cancer with adjacent-organ invasion

cues.phrase: tumor entering the splenic hilum
cues.why: Nearly names the organ to remove.

cues.phrase: The pancreatic tail separated along a soft tissue plane with an intact surface.
cues.why: Nearly names the organ to preserve. With the four binary combinations, the two sentences directly assemble the key.

fairness: The intended splenectomy with pancreatic preservation is defensible if the operative observations establish splenic-hilar involvement and no pancreatic invasion. The balanced matrix avoids convergence, but the case gives both component conclusions almost explicitly.

Importance: useful gastric-cancer principle against unnecessary adjacent-organ resection. Realism: discussing an intraoperative assessment as the 'operative plan' in clinic is temporally awkward; frame it clearly as retrospective review. Too easy for residents; no independent second decision is required.
suggestions: Use an actual uncertainty in adjacent-organ adherence or invasion and compare concrete oncologic plans that require interpreting that finding. Do not invent a reason to sacrifice an uninvolved organ.
Alternatively retain as an explicitly accepted foundational organ-preservation item. Clarify that the operative findings are being reviewed after surgery.

decisionNodes.stem: Which operative plan best fits Victor James's recorded interface findings?

answerChoices.label: En-bloc gastrectomy and distal pancreatectomy/splenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Prior represented pancreatic invasion plus a persistent inseparable bridge makes peeling through that interface an oncologic compromise; the represented margins support an en-bloc local plan.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy after pancreatic-plane separation; retain spleen
answerChoices.rationale: A radiographic response does not establish that an inseparable previously invaded interface is safe to divide through.

answerChoices.label: Palliative gastrojejunostomy with gastric tumor left in situ
answerChoices.rationale: This is credible when disease cannot be cleared or distant disease prevents the intended curative operation, neither of which follows from the recorded local bridge.

decisionNodes.explanation: A smaller radiographic interface after treatment does not prove that previously represented direct invasion has become safe to peel apart. In the specified locally resectable setting, plan en-bloc removal rather than divide through the persistent bridge or infer unresectability from adjacency itself. This is a retrospective extent decision, not a claim that every adherent proximal gastric cancer requires multivisceral resection.

priorIndependentReview.title: Mammographic mass morphology
fairness: Mass B is the best priority: the learner must interpret suspicious morphology in light of interval change and surgical-bed stability rather than choose high density or palpability alone. Each competing target has a plausible concerning feature, and the same action is offered at each site.

Importance: high-yield breast-workup reasoning. Realism: radiologist correlation and interval comparison are credible in surgical clinic. A table is appropriate for the longitudinal comparison, though it is not a substitute for a validated visual-morphology exercise.

Priority is defensible, but it does not establish that the enlarging palpable mass C needs no sampling. The unspecified magnitude and interval of growth limit any stronger claim about C; no confident key error identified for the narrowly prioritized task.
suggestions: Keep the task limited to priority and have clinical sign-off explicitly retain any separate workup needed for C. Do not convert this into a single-biopsy-only policy.

concept.learningObjective: Integrate a mass's shape and margin rather than density when deciding which mammographic finding needs diagnostic tissue assessment.
concept.novelty: Preserves the existing unadmitted morphology identity; the active core-biopsy objective starts after a suspicious target is identified.
concept.conceptVersionReason: Same scored clinical decision and stable FSRS identity; new observations/options require application rather than the earlier recall or cue shortcut.
concept.historyMigration: None. Preserved meanings retain IDs; materially changed constructs use new IDs and leave old histories intact.

decisionNodes.stem: Which target should be prioritized for image-guided core sampling in Nora Bennett's workup?

answerChoices.label: Image-guided core sampling of mass B
answerChoices.rationale: The newly radiating contour at the nonoperative site is the leading suspicious target; equal density does not negate that morphology.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided core sampling of mass A
answerChoices.rationale: The same concerning words require comparison with the established surgical-bed contour; they do not make this unchanged scar-centered target the first priority over B.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided core sampling of mass C
answerChoices.rationale: Growth and palpability need appropriate assessment, but do not override B's newly developed irregular spiculated morphology merely because C has high density.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret morphology with interval and site correlation, then prioritize the new suspicious target for tissue. Two rows have the same suspicious descriptors, and more than one finding deserves assessment; this priority choice does not declare the other masses benign or finish the patient's management.

priorIndependentReview.title: Calcification morphology and distribution

cues.phrase: No target calcifications in specimen; clip anterior to the mapped group
cues.why: Only group A is explicitly unsampled; the task asks which group needs renewed targeting. A reader can match missing target to repeat sampling without interpreting calcification morphology.

cues.phrase: Target calcifications present; clip centered on the sampled group
cues.why: Both competing groups are explicitly described as successfully targeted; their pathology also explains the calcifications. This completes option-by-option elimination.

fairness: Repeat targeting of A is appropriate, but morphology and the DCIS diagnosis are largely unnecessary to identify the stated technical miss. The answer follows from specimen coverage alone.

Importance: high-yield radiology-pathology concordance. Realism: specimen radiographs and clip maps are appropriate; clip location by itself can be misleading, but absent target calcifications independently supports inadequacy here. Too easy for PGY-2/3 residents.
suggestions: Test a genuine concordance decision after apparently successful sampling, with plausible competing interpretations of what was represented, rather than making only one row explicitly miss its target.
Keep specimen calcification data and avoid treating clip displacement alone as proof of failed acquisition. Remove redundant reassurance for the other rows unless it changes the decision.

decisionNodes.stem: Which group most warrants repeat representative sampling before Elena Torres's treatment plan is finalized?

answerChoices.label: Repeat vacuum sampling of group A
answerChoices.rationale: Specimen calcium confirms calcium acquisition, but arterial-wall calcium does not explain the target's nonvascular branching ductal pattern. This is a concordance problem after apparent technical success.

answerChoices.label: Repeat vacuum sampling of group B
answerChoices.rationale: The rim appearance and oil-cavity wall histology provide a coherent benign explanation. Benign wording is not itself a reason to resample.

answerChoices.label: Repeat vacuum sampling of group C
answerChoices.rationale: The tissue explains the suspicious calcification target. Its malignancy requires treatment planning but does not make repeat diagnostic acquisition the priority over the unexplained target.

decisionNodes.explanation: Calcium in a specimen and an appropriately placed clip do not by themselves establish radiology-pathology concordance. Compare what produced the calcification histologically with its imaged morphology. Group A remains unexplained, whereas B and C have findings that account for their patterns. Renew representative sampling of A before basing the treatment extent on a benign label.

clinicalCase.presentation: Maya Ellis, a 36-year-old woman who is not pregnant or breastfeeding, returns to clinic after diagnostic mammography and targeted ultrasound of her right-breast lump. The radiologist scanned the palpable 3-o'clock site with the examining clinician's marker in place. Both studies show no mass or distortion at that site.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next diagnostic plan best fits Maya Ellis's current finding?

answerChoices.label: Palpation-guided core needle biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: A persistent clinically suspicious finding still requires tissue diagnosis despite correctly targeted negative imaging; the lack of an image target supports palpation guidance.

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced breast MRI review
answerChoices.rationale: MRI can have selected roles but should not replace indicated tissue diagnosis of the persistent suspicious palpable target.

answerChoices.label: Short-interval targeted ultrasound review
answerChoices.rationale: Surveillance is credible for a clinically low-suspicion finding with reassuring correlation; that is not the examination trajectory here.

decisionNodes.explanation: The earlier study addressed the correct site. The remaining discrepancy is between a persistent suspicious examination and negative imaging, not a wrong referral location. Obtain tissue, using palpation guidance when no image target is visible. Negative mammography and targeted ultrasound do not erase a clinically concerning mass.

fairness: B is uniquely correct under the provided policy and constructed maps. Fairness is achieved by turning the exercise into reading comprehension rather than resident-level clinical reasoning.

Importance: complete benign-phyllodes excision is useful, but this policy/map exercise has lower incremental yield within a batch containing numerous phyllodes margin items. suggestions: Merge with a postoperative specimen-completeness decision or test a clinically meaningful capsular/extent uncertainty using comparable specific surgical plans.

decisionNodes.stem: Which completion-excision extent best fits Clara Morgan's postoperative record?

answerChoices.label: Focused re-excision of the retained segment
answerChoices.rationale: The concern is represented transection and residual tumor, not an inked intact capsule. A focused completion excision addresses that residual segment.

answerChoices.label: Circumferential cavity re-excision for a fixed 10-mm rim
answerChoices.rationale: This imports a malignant-phyllodes planning aim into a benign lesion and removes tissue beyond the represented residual segment.

answerChoices.label: Central breast re-excision including the nipple-areolar complex
answerChoices.rationale: This treats a nipple-side location as demonstrated nipple involvement. The record localizes residual tumor to the cavity edge, not the nipple itself.

decisionNodes.explanation: Benign phyllodes does not require a fixed-width rim merely because tumor touches ink. Here, however, the lesion was transected and a matching segment remains. Focused completion excision addresses a different problem from widening an intact benign capsule margin. Imaging is used to localize the represented residual segment, not to diagnose a new mass by appearance alone.

fairness: Lateral re-excision follows the supplied policy and final site-specific report. The superior shave is described as covering the full face, so there is no demonstrated residual ambiguity. However, the item counts an interpretation already performed by the pathologist as learner reasoning.

Importance: useful margin reconciliation, but repetitive within this phyllodes-heavy batch. Realism: an oriented reconciliation is credible; exact combined margin reporting needs pathologist confirmation. Too easy for residents.
suggestions: Test a real specimen-orientation or coverage discrepancy that changes the remaining operation, using clinically validated reporting conventions. Do not simply delete a necessary final margin and ask the learner to invent one.
Alternatively merge the borderline target and close-margin items into one meaningful planning decision. Keep any policy needed for fairness, but avoid a task solvable by reading one final number.

decisionNodes.stem: Which re-excision extent best fits Diane Porter's posterior findings?

answerChoices.label: Posterior re-excision to the fascia

answerChoices.rationale: This treats proximity to the chest wall as proof that muscle is the involved remaining boundary.

decisionNodes.explanation: The posterior margin and actual remaining boundary must be considered together. Do not generalize this to a case already excised to bare muscle or one with direct muscle invasion.

cues.why: Deliberately targets the object the stem just placed outside the node; this is an obvious wrong-target choice without needing medical knowledge.

fairness: A properly targeted needle biopsy is defensible. The combination of clip location and no nodal tissue supports a failed sample; the problem is not missing data but a caricatured surgical alternative. True excision of the enlarging node could be a reasonable competing approach, depending on accessibility and diagnostic needs.
Importance: high-value general specimen-target concordance principle, more useful than phyllodes-specific recall. Realism: an off-target needle sample is plausible. Too easy as currently phrased.
suggestions: Offer actual node excision rather than excision of a known misplaced clip, and supply accessibility/architecture needs that allow a defensible comparison with repeat image-guided biopsy.
Keep the inadequate-sample evidence; make the next action a real choice instead of restating the missed target.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next tissue-acquisition plan best fits Leah Carter's axillary record?

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the node
answerChoices.rationale: A representative needle tissue sample can supply additional material and histologic relationships before a more invasive operation in a deep axillary position.

answerChoices.label: Repeat FNA with on-site cell-block preparation
answerChoices.rationale: This can improve an acellular or poorly prepared aspirate, but the issue here is unresolved tissue classification after actual atypical cells were obtained.

answerChoices.label: Open excision biopsy of the deep axillary node
answerChoices.rationale: Excision may be appropriate if needle tissue remains inadequate or a process requires the whole node, but it need not precede a representative core in this specified setting.

decisionNodes.explanation: Phyllodes makes routine axillary staging uncommon, but it does not explain away a growing atypical node. priorIndependentReview.title: Malignant phyllodes operative margin target

cues.phrase: Malignant: aim 10 mm; below 5 mm supports re-excision.
cues.why: Gives the initial target directly; reading the minimum rim in each row is sufficient.

cues.phrase: while avoiding the additional chest-wall resection shown
cues.why: The task explicitly rules out map C, the only row naming an additional pectoral-muscle segment.

cues.phrase: Breast tissue plus the planned posterior extension
cues.why: The key is presented as the middle amount of tissue removal, exactly matching the instructed target-without-extra-sacrifice rule.

fairness: B is uniquely selected by the stipulated map and policy, but no medical reasoning is required. The difference between initial counseling aim and postoperative re-excision threshold is useful; here the stem and task do all of that interpretation.

Importance: limited incremental value beside the borderline-target and malignant-close-margin items. Realism: posterior tissue planes are insufficiently defined to generalize whether a specified extra rim is achievable without chest-wall resection. Too easy.
suggestions: Replace the explicit avoidance instruction with a neutral operative-planning task and a clinically grounded posterior-plane problem.

Consider merging the initial-target and postoperative-margin distinction into one clinically realistic case. Do not create difficulty by hiding the applicable policy or pretending an exact planned rim guarantees final clearance.

qualityReview.singleBestAnswer: The malignant tumor reaches the fascial boundary but represented muscle signal/motion do not show invasion; the supported draft plan includes fascia rather than capsule-only or automatic muscle removal.
qualityReview.closestError: Treat all deep contact as muscle invasion, or apply the benign capsular-excision goal to malignant phyllodes.
qualityReview.counterfactual: Direct muscle extension would change the deep component; a benign lesion with an intact removable capsule would change the margin goal.

statementMapping.constructedDataBasis: Fictional patient measurements, chronology, pathology and acquisition records; not empirical rates, universal treatment cutoffs or medication doses. Laboratory intervals are those of the constructed record.
statementMapping.extensionLimitations: Unchanged atoms retain original dates. Explicit offline extensions and option rankings carry targeted verification holds; no source retrieval or clinical sign-off.

sourceVerificationHolds.limitation: The recorded atoms establish margin aims/actions, not the exact fascia-versus-muscle operation. Directly verify both posterior-plane option rankings; no claim of verified fascia/muscle equivalence.

priorIndependentReview.title: Phyllodes dissemination pattern
fairness: The learner must recognize that a distant lesion can change curative-intent breast planning, then prioritize tissue that distinguishes metastasis from a separate lung primary. Prior lung adenocarcinoma makes histology genuinely consequential; the three choices are parallel tissue acquisitions.

Importance: high-yield oncologic staging principle, though the phyllodes-specific setting is uncommon. Realism: clinic staging before proposed local treatment is credible. A peripheral pulmonary target makes image-guided acquisition plausible without an artificial availability assurance.

Pulmonary sampling is the best priority among these options if technically feasible. Actual lesion size, accessibility and biopsy risk would matter in practice, and staging other suspicious sites is not excluded. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline.
suggestions: Retain the competing prior malignancy and curative-intent consequence. At clinical sign-off, confirm that the proposed lung target is safely accessible and that priority does not imply abandoning the node or breast-bed workup.

concept.learningObjective: Use phyllodes spread biology and the actual interval targets to select representative tissue for a new distant-staging question without assuming pulmonary origin from imaging.
concept.novelty: Adds an unadmitted disease-specific spread objective; axillary staging and general stage-versus-grade do not assess this route inference.
concept.conceptVersionReason: The original classified a route after origin was supplied. This version selects representative tissue for an unresolved distant staging question without presuming metastatic origin.
concept.historyMigration: None. Preserved meanings retain IDs; materially changed constructs use new IDs and leave old histories intact.

Tissue from the selected target will be compared with both prior tumors.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided core biopsy of the pulmonary target
answerChoices.rationale: Representative distant-lesion tissue addresses whether the proposed local operation is being planned in a metastatic setting and which prior tumor, if either, the lesion represents.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided core biopsy of the axillary target
answerChoices.rationale: This abnormal regional target also deserves assessment, but its tissue cannot establish the identity of the separate pulmonary finding or settle the distant-stage uncertainty.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided core biopsy of the operative-bed target
answerChoices.rationale: This may establish local recurrence, but a local result cannot determine whether the pulmonary lesion is distant phyllodes, recurrent lung carcinoma or another process.

decisionNodes.explanation: All three targets are abnormal, so this is not a choice between a new lesion and two reassurances. Before a curative-intent local operation, the distant lesion's identity is pivotal. Phyllodes can spread hematogenously, but the history of a separate lung primary prevents assigning origin from location or the breast history. Obtain representative pulmonary tissue for comparison; regional/local workup may still be needed and cannot substitute for that result.

priorIndependentReview.title: Overt renin-independent aldosterone production

cues.phrase: CT-directed unilateral adrenalectomy planning
cues.why: This option extends beyond the task's 'endocrine testing pathway' into an operation and can be partly rejected by category. It does not distinguish the key from the credible suppression-testing alternative.

cues.phrase: Potassium was corrected and interfering medicines were managed for his endocrine testing.
cues.why: An interpreted preparation assurance removes potential assay confounders. It is a fair boundary for this downstream objective, but it means the learner is not being tested on preparation adequacy.

fairness: The consequential distinctions are whether this overt biochemical phenotype warrants bypassing suppression testing and whether imaging can replace functional lateralization before surgery. Exact assay-dependent criteria make this a challenging PGY-2/3 item, not merely a diagnosis-label match.

Importance: high-yield endocrine-surgery pathway selection. Realism: explicit surgical preference is relevant because it changes the value of lateralization testing; it is not gratuitous preference cueing.

The key is defensible under the intended overt-phenotype pathway. Current assay-specific thresholds and exceptions were not independently verified because network use is prohibited; Melissa must confirm them. The category cue above does not determine the answer between the two actual testing sequences. Preserve the frozen version.
suggestions: Retain the exact frozen item and flag the testing-versus-operative-planning category limitation for future manager review. Do not imply that CT alone establishes unilateral functional disease or that this editorial PASS clinically approves the numerical criteria.

concept.learningObjective: Apply the recorded overt-phenotype exception to additional aldosterone suppression testing before surgical localization.
concept.novelty: Tests the intervening decision about whether suppression confirmation adds value, rather than obtaining the screening ratio or choosing a side for surgery.

priorIndependentReview.title: Factor assessment after an inhibitory mixing pattern
fairness: Immediate correction followed by loss of correction after incubation, with a normal incubated control, requires interpretation of a time-dependent inhibitory pattern. The next panel then tests the specific clinically plausible inhibitor rather than assuming a simple factor deficiency or choosing lupus-anticoagulant testing reflexively.

Importance: high-yield perioperative coagulation and acquired bleeding-disorder assessment. Realism: bruising, a peripheral redraw and laboratory interference checks fit preoperative evaluation; hematology involvement is appropriate.

Factor VIII activity plus inhibitor testing is the defensible priority. The mixing result is not itself definitive diagnosis, and lupus-anticoagulant testing can still be useful in a broader workup. Parallel panels and shared factor VIII testing avoid length/category/convergence cues. No definite clinical error identified offline.
suggestions: Retain the immediate/incubated/control pattern and frame the selected panel as the next priority with hematology, not the only testing ever needed.

priorIndependentReview.title: New swelling despite established lymphedema

cues.phrase: the femoral and popliteal segments were not examined because the requested study was a limited calf protocol
cues.why: Explicitly names the missing proximal coverage, while the key is 'Complete proximal-leg venous duplex ultrasound'. The absent-coverage-to-complete-test match solves the item.

cues.phrase: New thigh tenderness and increased whole-leg circumference
cues.why: Repeats the proximal distribution already described in the presentation, reinforcing the only proximal-leg test over two pelvic studies.

fairness: Prompt proximal venous assessment is defensible despite chronic lymphedema. The calf-only protocol is an unusual way to describe a DVT exclusion study and needs realism review; an actual acquisition record should justify it rather than invent a conspicuous omission for the question.

Importance: very high-yield avoidance of diagnostic anchoring after surgery. Realism: clinic escalation can be appropriate, but a symptomatic postoperative patient needs a prompt pathway. No definite key error; difficulty is too low because both distractors bypass the directly identified missing examination.
suggestions: Use a realistic ultrasound acquisition/quality discrepancy with competing investigations appropriate to the same unresolved vascular problem.

Keep the necessary new symptoms and study coverage, but avoid an explicit 'not examined' statement functioning as the entire answer. Do not replace valid coverage evidence with vague 'negative scan' wording.

priorIndependentReview.title: Symptom control versus thyroid-hormone production

cues.phrase: Since starting propranolol her pulse and tremor have improved, but free T4 remains above the laboratory interval.
cues.why: Provides the symptom-versus-hormone contrast almost as a teaching sentence; simply increasing the same symptom drug is a weak competing plan.

cues.phrase: has not started another thyroid treatment
cues.why: An explicit missing-treatment cue points to initiating the only new nonradioactive thyroid medicine.

fairness: Methimazole is a defensible treatment to address ongoing Graves hyperthyroidism, subject to clinical review. The task is not a full perioperative optimization plan and does not establish readiness for elective surgery.

Importance: high-yield endocrine/perioperative principle. Realism: endocrine coordination is appropriate. Breastfeeding is a legitimate constraint and must remain; the issue is the weak pair of competitors, not the presence of the constraint. Too easy for residents: two familiar facts do not create two consequential reasoning steps here.
undefined Lactation makes the radioiodine option a clinically excluded competitor; recognizing that requires medical knowledge, so it is a difficulty weakness rather than a purely lexical cue.
suggestions: Compare credible antithyroid or perioperative plans using an actual response trajectory or treatment limitation, with all choices addressing hormone control at the same stage.
Retain lactation status and necessary treatment history, but replace the already-effective symptom-drug escalation and contraindicated treatment as easy foils.

qualityReview.coverKeyAttack: Every choice adjusts the same two medicines; no new-drug-versus-effective-symptom-drug cue or contraindicated radioiodine option. The result table contains observations rather than an authored symptom/hormone lesson.
qualityReview.sameStageAndCategory: Three current two-medicine adjustment plans.
qualityReview.interpretFindings: Distinguish lagging TSH from ongoing free-hormone excess and identify a clinical effect of continued beta blockade.
qualityReview.applyFindings: Avoid unnecessary antithyroid escalation while reducing the symptom drug rather than stopping disease therapy.
qualityReview.difficultyReason: Requires interpreting discordant follow-up assays and choosing which component to adjust, with two credible common errors.
qualityReview.singleBestAnswer: Both free hormones are in range and the patient now has a symptomatic slow pulse; the draft plan retains antithyroid therapy and reduces beta blockade.
qualityReview.closestError: Escalate methimazole for suppressed TSH, or stop it because on-treatment hormone levels are normal.
qualityReview.counterfactual: Persistently elevated free hormones would reopen dose escalation; documented remission would change the withdrawal discussion.

reviewerResponse.cues: Removes explicit missing antithyroid treatment and the already-effective drug/contraindicated radioiodine foils.

answerChoices.label: Maintain methimazole and reduce propranolol

answerChoices.label: Increase methimazole and maintain propranolol

priorIndependentReview.title: IVC filter versus anticoagulation for a provoked DVT

cues.phrase: with no therapeutic regimen entered
cues.why: Names the missing action directly; the key starts 'Therapeutic enoxaparin'.

cues.phrase: Preventive enoxaparin with a retrievable IVC filter
cues.why: Pairs a newly documented clot with the same prevention category already described, making an obviously incomplete treatment foil.

fairness: Therapeutic anticoagulation without routine filter placement is defensible for the supplied postoperative proximal DVT. However, exact enoxaparin selection assumes suitable renal function and no relevant heparin contraindication; those are not provided. The multiple no-bleeding observations are legitimate anticoagulation-safety context, but together they remove the main filter rationale rather than create a close competing decision.

Importance: very high-yield postoperative VTE management. Realism: appropriate hospital escalation; new unilateral symptoms and objective ultrasound are coherent. Too easy once active bleeding and limb threat have both been explicitly neutralized; the dominant rule is anticoagulate an established clot.
suggestions: Use an actual anticoagulation constraint, interruption or apparent treatment-failure question with sufficient dosing/renal/bleeding context to compare plausible plans.
Do not remove safety observations to make filter use ambiguous. If retaining this as a basic VTE safety decision, seek explicit acceptance of that role.

priorIndependentReview.title: Investigating oxygen-carrying capacity

cues.phrase: Copied from the preoperative sample into the postoperative calculation
cues.why: Flags the only stale input explicitly; the sole choice measuring that input is the CBC.

cues.phrase: before attributing his fatigue to persistent pulmonary oxygenation failure
cues.why: The task tells the reader to seek the nonpulmonary alternative, making both gas-related distractors less attractive even without interpreting oxygen content.

cues.phrase: Within the reporting laboratory interval
cues.why: The existing arterial oxygen result partly disposes of the ABG competitor; the normal saturation supplies a second reassurance in the same direction.

answerChoices.rationale: Normal oxygenation does not establish normal oxygen content. The current low hemoglobin and pre-existing small-cell pattern support evaluating iron status rather than attributing everything to the inpatient lung event.

answerChoices.rationale: This can investigate a suspected oxygenation/dyshemoglobin problem, but the present room-air measurements and red-cell trajectory identify a more supported initial assessment.

cues.phrase: Contrast CT shows a percutaneous route to its solid portion

cues.phrase: the pathologist requests intact tissue relationships

fairness: Image-guided core biopsy is plausible for an accessible deep node when further architecture is needed. Open excision can also be justified for some suspected lymphoid processes; the requested degree of architecture and local pathology expectations would affect adequacy.

Importance: useful tissue-acquisition judgment within general surgery. Realism: deep-node procedural risk is real, but the paired access/risk sentences and least-invasive task are heavily engineered to select core. Too easy as written; do not claim core is universally sufficient for lymphoma classification.
suggestions: Ask a neutral next-biopsy decision with a specific unresolved diagnostic requirement and comparable realistic acquisition plans.

Retain true anatomical risk and access observations, but remove rationale-like feasibility permission and the leading 'least invasive' instruction unless invasiveness itself is the explicitly accepted basic objective.

clinicalCase.displayName: Tissue sampling after inadequate neck FNA
clinicalCase.presentation: George Adams, a 66-year-old man, returns to clinic with a persistent enlarging cervical lymph node deep to the sternocleidomastoid. Two ultrasound-guided FNAs have yielded viable lymphoid cells. Flow testing identifies an abnormal population, but the cell-block sections contain dispersed cells and the report cannot classify the process. Contrast CT places the node behind the internal jugular vein and against the carotid sheath.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next biopsy plan best fits George Adams's diagnostic record?

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: The aspirates obtained cells and flow information but did not resolve tissue classification. Representative core tissue is a selected next step before deep open excision.

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided FNA biopsy with on-site preparation
answerChoices.rationale: This improves cell yield or preparation, but the existing aspirates already contain viable abnormal cells and ancillary results; it may repeat the same material limitation.

answerChoices.label: Open cervical node excision biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: Excision may be required for a whole-node architectural question or after inadequate core, but it is not automatically the next procedure for this deep selected mass.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret what the aspirates did provide before repeating them. Actual viable abnormal cells and completed flow testing do not guarantee that dispersed-cell material can resolve the remaining classification. Core biopsy is a selected next tissue approach in this deep anatomical setting. Some lymphoid processes still require excision; the item does not make core universally sufficient for lymphoma.
sourceLabels: Head and Neck Cancer: United Kingdom National Multidisciplinary Guidelines, Sixth Edition

decisionNodes.stem: Which ventilatory response best fits Andrew Cook's paired arterial record?

answerChoices.label: Increase alveolar ventilation; recheck arterial gas
answerChoices.rationale: The rising CO2 adds a respiratory acidifying component to the pre-existing alkalosis. A near-reference pH does not establish adequate ventilation; delivered ventilation has fallen.

answerChoices.label: Maintain ventilator settings; repeat arterial analysis
answerChoices.rationale: This treats the later pH as evidence of satisfactory ventilation and misses the offsetting disorders and fall in delivered volume.

answerChoices.label: Reduce respiratory frequency; reassess the blood gas
answerChoices.rationale: This treats the elevated bicarbonate as compensation for chronic CO2 retention or assumes the current CO2 needs further permissive elevation.

decisionNodes.explanation: The initial high bicarbonate and alkalemia precede the CO2 rise. The later near-reference pH reflects offsetting contributions, not proof that ventilation is satisfactory. The acute CO2 change with reduced delivered volume supports increasing effective alveolar ventilation and checking the response. This does not prescribe a respiratory rate, tidal volume, universal CO2 target or substitute for checking the airway/circuit and other causes.

priorIndependentReview.title: Reassessing a changing hand burn

cues.phrase: He reports less pain
cues.why: Directly weakens analgesia-focused reassessment, one of only two competitors.

cues.phrase: Burn-center depth and transfer reassessment
cues.why: The key uniquely addresses lesion severity and escalation; the alternatives address comfort or exercises rather than a competing interpretation of the changing wound.

fairness: Updated specialist depth review is sensible. The outer healing versus central deterioration distinction is important, but the task already guarantees burn-center review and asks only which generic topic to emphasize. It does not establish whether transfer, urgent in-person review or a local-care change is actually needed. The pale, dry, minimally blanching and less sensitive center is a straightforward depth-recognition cluster for residents; these necessary findings should remain.

Importance: high-yield burn evolution and hand-function safety. Realism: reassessment during clinic follow-up is appropriate. Timing, extent and local capability would matter for an actual transfer decision. Too easy; all three topics can belong in the same burn review.
suggestions: Ask one concrete next care action and give the timing, distribution and facility context needed to rank credible escalation choices.
Preserve central depth warning signs; do not hide them for difficulty. Seek explicit safety-recognition acceptance if the aim is simply noticing deepening despite less pain.

The burn center initially reviewed photographs and arranged clinic dressings and hand exercises. The clinic has dressing and therapy services but no burn operating service. He can move his fingers, though the central wound pulls across the joints during flexion.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next care action best fits Thomas Wright's serial wound findings?

answerChoices.label: Arrange same-day burn-center surgical assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Central depth evolution over hand joints changes the assessment despite peripheral healing. Specialist assessment should determine excision/grafting and transfer needs.

answerChoices.label: Continue clinic dressings with scheduled hand therapy
answerChoices.rationale: This fits an uncomplicated healing superficial partial-thickness trajectory, but does not resolve the evolving central depth and joint-area concern.

answerChoices.label: Arrange urgent circumferential eschar-release surgery
answerChoices.rationale: Eschar release addresses a constricting perfusion/ventilation problem; depth over joints is not itself that indication.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the central wound separately from the healing edge. The changed surface, blanching and sensation raise a deeper injury concern across important hand joints, warranting prompt in-person burn surgical assessment. The specialist determines operative care and transfer rather than the clinic treating a less painful center as recovery. Depth alone does not establish a need for eschar release. No automatic transfer, graft date or burn-size threshold is invented.

The specialist determines operative care and transfer rather than the clinic treating a less painful center as recovery. Depth alone does not establish a need for eschar release. No automatic transfer, graft date or burn-size threshold is invented.

decisionNodes.stem: Which further reversal plan best fits Patrick King's recorded course?

answerChoices.label: Intravenous vitamin K with serial INR testing
answerChoices.rationale: Initial correction after PCC does not establish sustained restoration of vitamin-K-dependent production. Unreliable oral delivery and rebound without redosing support IV vitamin K rather than automatic repeat factor loading.

answerChoices.label: Repeat four-factor PCC with serial INR testing
answerChoices.rationale: This treats the later INR as proof that more rapid factor loading is required despite achieved hemostasis and an unresolved sustained-reversal component.

answerChoices.label: Plasma factor replacement with serial INR testing
answerChoices.rationale: Plasma can supply factors in emergency reversal, but it does not directly correct the unreliable vitamin-K component and adds volume without the current rapid-replacement indication.

decisionNodes.explanation: Do not infer durable reversal from an early INR after factor replacement. The observed emesis does not prove zero absorption, but it makes the oral dose unreliable; the later INR rise without warfarin redosing is consistent with an inadequately secured sustained-reversal component. In the represented controlled-bleeding stage, give IV phytonadione and follow the INR rather than reflexively repeat factor loading. New major bleeding or another urgent intervention would change the immediate replacement question.

cues.phrase: continued arterial extravasation into the abdomen
cues.why: Establishes ongoing major bleeding; the only immediate option is favored over two options expressly delaying reversal.

cues.why: Names the missing intervention that all options repeat, leaving only 'now' versus waiting.

fairness: Urgent factor replacement is a defensible principle in ongoing major warfarin-associated bleeding. However, 'above the laboratory interval' spans minimally elevated through markedly prolonged INR and is insufficiently precise for an exact reversal decision under many protocols; the actual INR and timing relative to vitamin K require clinician review.

Importance: very high-yield emergency reversal. Realism: simultaneous hemorrhage control matters; PCC cannot substitute for control of arterial bleeding. Too easy because the task and options have already selected the agent, leaving an obvious urgent-versus-delay decision.
suggestions: Provide the actual clinically relevant INR/administration chronology and source-supported protocol context without inventing a threshold.

decisionNodes.stem: Which rapid factor-replacement product should accompany intravenous vitamin K while hemorrhage control proceeds for Harold Evans?

answerChoices.label: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
answerChoices.rationale: This supplies the relevant vitamin-K-dependent factors rapidly with less infusion volume than plasma, while vitamin K supports the paired reversal strategy.

answerChoices.label: Thawed plasma for vitamin-K-dependent factor replacement
answerChoices.rationale: Plasma can supply factors, but further volume is a poor fit for the new congestion signs when selecting the preferred rapid reversal product.

answerChoices.label: Recombinant activated factor VII concentrate
answerChoices.rationale: A single-factor product does not supply the factor II, VII, IX and X replacement represented by four-factor PCC.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret both the medication-specific coagulopathy and the new volume burden. Four-factor PCC supplies the relevant factors with less infusion volume and faster preparation/administration than plasma, and IV vitamin K remains paired with it. The signs after plasma make continuing a large-volume strategy less attractive. Factor reversal accompanies hemorrhage control; it does not replace it. The INR is an observed case value, not a newly asserted universal cutoff.

decisionNodes.stem: Which rapid factor-replacement product should accompany intravenous vitamin K while hemorrhage control proceeds for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
answerChoices.rationale: This supplies the relevant vitamin-K-dependent factors rapidly with less infusion volume than plasma, while vitamin K supports the paired reversal strategy.

answerChoices.label: Thawed plasma for vitamin-K-dependent factor replacement
answerChoices.rationale: Plasma can supply factors, but further volume is a poor fit for the new congestion signs when selecting the preferred rapid reversal product.

answerChoices.label: Recombinant activated factor VII concentrate
answerChoices.rationale: A single-factor product does not supply the factor II, VII, IX and X replacement represented by four-factor PCC.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret both the medication-specific coagulopathy and the new volume burden. Four-factor PCC supplies the relevant factors with less infusion volume and faster preparation/administration than plasma, and IV vitamin K remains paired with it. The INR is an observed case value, not a newly asserted universal cutoff.

priorIndependentReview.title: Early nutrition after an extensive burn

cues.phrase: Low-rate enteral nutrition with tolerance checks
cues.why: The key uniquely offers cautious initiation of the physiologic route, whereas the alternatives choose primary PN or an explicit stool prerequisite. The reassuring row and 'with tolerance checks' make it the obvious cautious plan.

cues.phrase: Deferred nutritional delivery until stool passage
cues.why: States an absolute gating rule and offers no interim nutrition, making it a weak distractor for a resident.

fairness: The learner does perform two meaningful steps—recognize improving perfusion rather than rely on the earlier shock state, then choose enteral initiation despite quiet bowel sounds—but both are straightforward with these competitors. Too easy for the intended resident difficulty. The completely favorable second perfusion row is necessary data, not an unfair word-matching clue.

Importance: very high-yield burn/critical-care nutrition. Realism: improving perfusion and absence of concerning abdominal findings support cautious feeding. Extent of burn is not actually given in the presentation, despite the title; clinical review should confirm the nutritional indication and trajectory. No definite key error identified.
suggestions: Keep the actual perfusion trajectory and necessary gastrointestinal findings. Compare plausible enteral initiation/escalation strategies or a genuinely unresolved tolerance decision, rather than primary PN and fasting until stool.
If retained as a basic safety item, label and obtain acceptance of that purpose. Do not manufacture difficulty by removing evidence that shock has resolved.

decisionNodes.stem: Which feeding prescription best fits Zoe Turner's later hospital observations while urgent abdominal assessment proceeds?

answerChoices.label: Pause gastric feeding during abdominal reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: New hypoperfusion and abdominal warnings change the earlier eligibility for feeding; moving the tube does not resolve a possible intestinal perfusion problem.

answerChoices.label: Use postpyloric feeding during abdominal reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: A postpyloric route can address selected gastric delivery/intolerance problems, but does not bypass the need for adequate intestinal perfusion.

answerChoices.label: Maintain gastric feeding during abdominal reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Continuing low-rate delivery can fit stable tolerated feeding, but the new shock and abdominal trajectory are materially different from the earlier start conditions.

decisionNodes.explanation: An earlier successful resuscitation does not permanently establish enteral eligibility. The new support requirement, falling urine output and changed abdomen require holding enteral delivery while urgent resuscitation and abdominal evaluation proceed. Advancing the tube past the stomach does not establish intestinal safety. This does not set a universal vasopressor cutoff or mandate immediate PN during shock.

priorIndependentReview.title: Planned thoracic injury exposure

cues.phrase: posterior mid-thoracic esophageal wall defect
cues.why: The accessibility description directly matches the posterolateral component of the key. The visible image is also titled 'Thoracic localization - posterior orientation'.

cues.phrase: the azygos arch approaches the superior vena cava on the right
cues.why: Directly supplies the right-sided component. Combining 'posterior' and 'right' constructs the key from the four balanced options without substantive operative knowledge.

cues.phrase: A track runs down to a pool in the left pleural space.
cues.why: The description has already distinguished the left dependent pool from the actual defect, neutralizing the intended laterality trap before the resident interprets the image.

fairness: Right posterolateral exposure is defensible for the depicted esophageal and azygos targets in a stabilized patient. The image exists and is readable; the problem is that its description preinterprets the source-versus-pool distinction and the choice set makes simple directional matching sufficient.

Importance: useful trauma/esophageal exposure knowledge, though less commonly applied by a PGY-2/3 than the general perioperative items. Realism: retrospective injury localization is coherent. Contralateral pleural contamination may also need treatment; the question is only about exposure of the two repair targets, not a complete operation. Too easy.
suggestions: Retain accessible anatomical observations but avoid a description that narrates the intended source-versus-dependent-pool inference before it is tested.

Compare credible operative approaches requiring consequences of injury level, vascular involvement and physiological status, rather than merely concatenating side and orientation words. Do not remove safety or localization information needed for one best exposure.

clinicalCase.presentation: Nathan Scott, a 42-year-old man, reviews his penetrating chest-injury record in postoperative clinic. Initial imaging localized a middle thoracic esophageal injury and an azygos-region vascular injury. After a temporary response to blood replacement, a planned open repair was discussed. Before positioning he lost a palpable central pulse in the trauma resuscitation bay; the team began compressions immediately.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial chest exposure best fits the last stage of Nathan Scott's recorded course?

answerChoices.label: Left anterolateral thoracotomy
answerChoices.rationale: Traumatic arrest changes the first objective to immediate resuscitative chest access rather than optimal elective exposure of the previously localized repair targets.

answerChoices.label: Planned right posterolateral thoracotomy
answerChoices.rationale: This is a reasonable planned approach for the localized esophageal/azygos targets in a sufficiently stable patient, but not the initial positioning/exposure during the recorded arrest.

answerChoices.label: Median sternotomy with pericardial exploration
answerChoices.rationale: This is a credible operative exposure for selected central cardiac injuries, but it is not the standard initial resuscitative access represented by the traumatic-arrest pathway here.

decisionNodes.explanation: The earlier anatomy still matters for later repair, but the current objective is resuscitative access during traumatic arrest. An anterior resuscitative approach takes priority over lateral positioning for planned posterior-target repair; extension depends on findings and the local trauma protocol.
